ai.literal: To be respected they will not be subject to, glory they will lose, always, liquor desire having, those who live.
ai.translation: Those who live with an abiding desire for liquor will never command the respect of others, and they will lose their reputation for all time.
ai.modern: மதுவின் மீது விருப்பம் கொண்டு வாழ்பவர்கள், எப்போதும் பிறரால் மதிக்கப்பட மாட்டார்கள்; தங்களுடைய புகழையும் இழப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet introduces the chapter on avoiding liquor by highlighting the social consequences of addiction. The poet states that those who live with a constant desire for alcohol will lose two essential elements of a dignified life: the respect of others and their own personal glory. The word 'உட்கு' refers to the awe-inspired respect or fear that a person of dignity commands, which an addict loses completely. This loss of esteem and reputation is not temporary but persists at all times, as indicated by 'எஞ்ஞான்றும்'.

ai.literal: Do not drink liquor; if drinking, let them drink, those who do not wish to be esteemed by noble people.
ai.translation: Do not drink liquor. If one must drink, let it be only those who do not care to be held in esteem by noble minds.
ai.modern: கள்ளைக் குடிக்கக் கூடாது. ஒருவேளை குடிக்க வேண்டும் என்றால், சான்றோர்களால் மதிக்கப்படுவதை விரும்பாதவர்கள் மட்டும் குடிக்கட்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet advises against the consumption of alcohol by highlighting its social consequences. It states that if anyone wishes to drink liquor, it should only be those who have no desire to be respected or thought highly of by wise and noble people. The word 'சான்றோரான்' refers to the noble and virtuous, whose esteem is highly valued in society. The term 'எண்ணப்பட' means to be thought of or esteemed. Thus, the poet emphasizes that drinking liquor completely destroys one's reputation among the wise.

ai.literal: Even in the face of the mother who gave birth, [drunkenness] is unpleasant indeed; what then [will it be] in the face of the noble?
ai.translation: If drunkenness is offensive even in the presence of one's own mother, how much more shameful must it be in the presence of the wise and noble?
ai.modern: பெற்ற தாயின் முன்னிலையிலேயே மது மயக்கம் வெறுக்கத்தக்கது என்றால், அறிவு ஒழுக்கங்களில் சிறந்த சான்றோர்களின் முன்னிலையில் அது எவ்வளவு இழிவானதாக இருக்கும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute disgrace of intoxication by comparing its effect on two highly respected figures: one's mother and the wise. A mother's love is unconditional, yet even she cannot bear to look at her child in a drunken state; it brings her pain and disgust. If the most forgiving person finds it intolerable, the couplet asks rhetorically, how much worse will it appear to the noble and virtuous ('சான்றோர்') who judge by high moral standards? Thus, the poet emphasizes that drunkenness destroys one's dignity in the eyes of everyone, from closest family to society's finest.

ai.literal: Modesty called good woman back will give to those of the not-cherished great fault called liquor.
ai.translation: The virtuous maiden called Modesty will turn her back and depart from those who commit the undesirable, grave crime of drinking liquor.
ai.modern: நாணம் என்று சொல்லப்படும் நல்ல பெண்மகள், கள் குடித்தல் என்னும் விரும்பத்தகாத பெரும் குற்றத்தைச் செய்பவர்களுக்குத் தன் முதுகைக் காட்டி விலகிப் போவாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet personifies modesty as a virtuous woman who abandons those who drink liquor. The poet describes drinking as an undesirable, grave vice (பேணா பெருங்குற்றம்) that strips a person of their dignity. When a person consumes alcohol, they lose their self-control and sense of shame, symbolized by the lady of Modesty turning her back (புறங்கொடுக்கும்) on them. Thus, the desire for liquor drives away one's innate decency and self-respect.

ai.literal: Giving wealth and buying the unconsciousness of one's body indeed possesses the character of utter helplessness.
ai.translation: To pay away one's wealth to purchase the unconsciousness of one's own body is indeed the height of foolish helplessness.
ai.modern: பொருளைக் கொடுத்துத் தன் உடம்பை அறியாத மயக்க நிலையை விலைக்கு வாங்குவது, என்ன செய்வது என்று தெரியாத அறியாமைத் தன்மையைக் கொண்டதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet exposes the irrationality of drinking by framing it as a foolish commercial transaction. The poet describes the act of consuming alcohol as paying one's own wealth (poruḷ koṭuttu) to purchase physical unconsciousness or stupor (mey-y-aṟiyāmai koḷal). Such behavior is characterized as 'kai-y-aṟiyāmai', which denotes utter helplessness or a total lack of self-control. Through these contrasting terms of 'knowing' and 'not knowing', the verse shows how a person willingly spends resources to lose their basic physical awareness.

ai.literal: Those who sleep than those who are dead different are not; at all times, poison those who drink are those who drink liquor.
ai.translation: Those who sleep are no different from the dead; likewise, those who drink liquor are, at all times, no different from those who drink poison.
ai.modern: உறங்குபவர்கள் இறந்தவர்களை விட வேறுபட்டவர்கள் அல்லர்; அதுபோல, கள் குடிப்பவர்கள் எப்போதும் நஞ்சு குடிப்பவர்களே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a powerful double analogy to warn against the consumption of alcohol. First, it equates sleep with death, noting that a sleeping person is temporarily as inactive and unaware as a dead person. Second, it equates drinking liquor with drinking poison, showing that those who consume alcohol are effectively destroying their own lives. By comparing the drunkard to a poison-drinker and the sleeper to the dead, the poet emphasizes that alcohol consumption is a form of slow, self-inflicted destruction of consciousness and life.

ai.literal: Having their secrets detected, by the local townspeople they will be laughed at always, those who drink liquor secretly and lose their awareness.
ai.translation: Those who drink liquor secretly and lose their senses will have their secrets found out and will be laughed at by their fellow-townsmen at all times.
ai.modern: ரகசியமாகக் கள் குடித்துத் தன் அறிவை இழப்பவர்கள், எப்போதும் தம் ஊர் மக்களால் அவர்களின் ரகசியங்கள் அறியப்பட்டு எள்ளி நகையாடப்படுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the illusion of secret drinking. The poet explains that those who drink liquor in secret ('kaḷ oṟṟi') and lose their mental clarity or droop their eyes ('kaṇ cāypavar') cannot keep it a secret for long. Their inner secrets will be easily detected ('uḷ oṟṟi') by others because of their drunken behavior. Consequently, they will be mocked and laughed at ('nakappaṭuvar') by their own local townspeople ('uḷḷūr') at all times ('eññāṉṟum').

ai.literal: Abandon the saying 'I do not know being intoxicated'; even that which was hidden in the heart will increase at that very moment.
ai.translation: Abandon the boast, 'I have never lost my senses to drink'; for when you drink, even the secrets hidden deep within your heart will be magnified and exposed.
ai.modern: நான் மது அருந்தித் தன்மறதி அடைந்ததில்லை என்று சொல்வதைக் கைவிட வேண்டும். மது அருந்தும்போது, நெஞ்சில் ஒளித்து வைத்திருந்த இரகசியங்களும் அங்கே வெளிப்பட்டு மிகுதியாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the self-deception of those who drink but claim they never lose control or reveal their secrets. The poet advises such people to abandon the boast 'I have never known intoxication' (களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக). When a person drinks, the alcohol acts on the mind, and whatever was carefully hidden in the heart (நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்ததூஉம்) will be magnified and exposed at that very moment (ஆங்கே மிகும்). Thus, drinking inevitably betrays one's innermost secrets, making the claim of self-control impossible to maintain.

ai.literal: Showing reason to him who is drunk is like searching for him who has dived under water with a fire torch.
ai.translation: Trying to reason with a drunkard is like taking a burning torch underwater to search for someone who has dived deep.
ai.modern: மது அருந்தி மயங்கியவனிடம் அறிவுரை கூறித் திருத்த முயல்வது, தண்ணீருக்குள் மூழ்கிய ஒருவனைத் தீப்பந்தம் கொண்டு தேடுவதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute futility of trying to reform or reason with someone who is heavily intoxicated. The poet uses a brilliant and humorous analogy: trying to guide a drunkard with logical arguments is like diving underwater with a burning torch to find someone. Just as water instantly extinguishes fire, the state of drunkenness completely drowns out any light of reason. The word 'turīi' refers to searching or probing, specifically with a light source, emphasizing the absurdity of using fire where it cannot survive. Therefore, attempting to counsel an intoxicated person is a completely pointless endeavor.

ai.literal: At the time of not drinking liquor, when seeing an intoxicated person, will he not think of the degradation of his own drinking?
ai.translation: When a man is sober and looks at someone who is drunk, will he not realize the utter degradation of his own drinking?
ai.modern: மது அருந்தாத நேரத்தில், குடித்துவிட்டு மயங்கிக் கிடப்பவனைப் பார்க்கும்போது, ஒருவன் தான் குடிப்பதால் ஏற்படும் அவமானத்தை நினைக்க மாட்டானா?
ai.explanation: This couplet offers a practical way for a drinker to reform. It suggests that when a person is sober, they should observe the shameful state of another person who is heavily intoxicated. Seeing the loss of dignity, speech, and self-control in someone else serves as a mirror. The observer will then inevitably realize the same degradation and embarrassment they themselves cause when they drink, prompting them to give up the habit.
